Phase 5: Geographic Overlay


OB-GYN Provider Network Analysis


---


Objective


Connect the network analysis from Phase 4 to real geography. This notebook answers the central project question: Do counties with weaker OB-GYN referral networks also have worse maternal health outcomes? We map providers to counties, aggregate network metrics geographically, overlay maternal morbidity rates, and identify the counties where virtual care models could have the greatest impact.


Inputs


| File | Source |

|------|--------|

| obgyn_providers_network.csv | Phase 4 — providers with centrality scores, tiers, communities |

| obgyn_edges_individuals.csv | Phase 2 — individual-to-individual shared patient pairs |

| county_morbidity_rates.csv | Phase 2 — CDC WONDER morbidity rates |

| state_network_metrics.csv | Phase 4 — state-level network aggregations |

| HUD USPS ZIP Crosswalk | Downloaded in this notebook — maps ZIP codes to county FIPS |


Outputs


| File | Description |

|------|-------------|

| county_network_morbidity.csv | County-level table joining network metrics with morbidity rates |

| target_counties.csv | High-morbidity + weak-network counties (virtual care opportunity) |


Sections


1. Setup & Load Data

2. ZIP-to-County FIPS Mapping

3. County-Level Network Metrics

4. Join with Morbidity Rates

5. Choropleth Maps

6. Regression Analysis

7. Target County Identification

8. Export & Summary

2. ZIP-to-County FIPS Mapping


Our provider data has 5-digit ZIP codes; our morbidity data has 5-digit county FIPS codes. ZIP codes and counties don't map 1:1 — a ZIP can span multiple counties. We use the HUD USPS ZIP Crosswalk to assign each provider's ZIP to its most probable county.


Approach: Download the HUD crosswalk (ZIP → County, with residential and business address ratios). For each ZIP, we assign the county with the highest tot_ratio (the county where the most addresses in that ZIP are located).


If the HUD crosswalk is unavailable, we fall back to a Census ZCTA-to-County relationship file.

In [3]:
# -------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2a. Build ZIP-to-County Crosswalk
# -------------------------------------------------------------------
# Option A: HUD crosswalk (if you downloaded it from
#   https://www.huduser.gov/portal/datasets/usps_crosswalk.html)
# Option B: Build a simple crosswalk from the NPPES state + ZIP data
#   combined with Census Bureau ZCTA-County relationship file.
#
# Since the HUD crosswalk requires an account, we use a pragmatic
# approach: download the Census Bureau's ZCTA-to-County relationship
# file for the 2010 Census (covers our 2015 study period).
# -------------------------------------------------------------------

CROSSWALK_URL = "https://www2.census.gov/geo/docs/maps-data/data/rel/zcta_county_rel_10.txt"
CROSSWALK_LOCAL = RAW_DIR / "zcta_county_rel_10.txt"

# Download if not already cached
if not CROSSWALK_LOCAL.exists():
    print(f"Downloading ZCTA-County crosswalk from Census Bureau...")
    import urllib.request
    urllib.request.urlretrieve(CROSSWALK_URL, CROSSWALK_LOCAL)
    print(f"Saved to: {CROSSWALK_LOCAL}")
else:
    print(f"Crosswalk already cached: {CROSSWALK_LOCAL}")

# Load crosswalk
crosswalk_raw = pd.read_csv(CROSSWALK_LOCAL, dtype=str)
print(f"\nCrosswalk loaded: {len(crosswalk_raw):,} rows")
print(f"Columns: {list(crosswalk_raw.columns)}")
display(crosswalk_raw.head(3))

In [4]:
# -------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2b. Clean Crosswalk: Map each ZCTA to its primary county
# -------------------------------------------------------------------
# The Census crosswalk has columns:
#   ZCTA5: 5-digit ZIP/ZCTA
#   STATE, COUNTY: state and county FIPS
#   GEOID: full 5-digit county FIPS (state + county)
#   POPPT: population in the ZCTA-county overlap
#   ZPOPPCT: % of the ZCTA's population in this county
#
# For each ZCTA, we keep the county with the highest population share.
# -------------------------------------------------------------------

crosswalk_raw["ZPOPPCT"] = pd.to_numeric(crosswalk_raw["ZPOPPCT"], errors="coerce")

# For each ZCTA, keep the row with the highest ZPOPPCT (primary county)
zip_to_county = (
    crosswalk_raw
    .sort_values("ZPOPPCT", ascending=False)
    .drop_duplicates(subset="ZCTA5", keep="first")
    [["ZCTA5", "GEOID", "STATE", "ZPOPPCT"]]
    .rename(columns={"ZCTA5": "zip5", "GEOID": "fips", "STATE": "state_fips"})
    .copy()
)

# Ensure FIPS is 5 digits (zero-padded)
zip_to_county["fips"] = zip_to_county["fips"].str.zfill(5)

print(f"ZIP-to-county crosswalk: {len(zip_to_county):,} unique ZIPs")
print(f"Median ZPOPPCT (confidence): {zip_to_county['ZPOPPCT'].median():.1f}%")
print(f"ZIPs with 100% in one county: {(zip_to_county['ZPOPPCT'] >= 100).sum():,}")
display(zip_to_county.head())

# -------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2c. Assign County FIPS to Each Provider
# -------------------------------------------------------------------

providers_geo = providers_net.merge(
    zip_to_county[["zip5", "fips"]],
    on="zip5",
    how="left"
)

matched = providers_geo["fips"].notna().sum()
unmatched = providers_geo["fips"].isna().sum()

print(f"Provider-to-county matching:")
print(f"  Matched:   {matched:,} ({matched/len(providers_geo)*100:.1f}%)")
print(f"  Unmatched: {unmatched:,} ({unmatched/len(providers_geo)*100:.1f}%)")
print(f"  Unique counties: {providers_geo['fips'].nunique():,}")

if unmatched > 0:
    print(f"\n  Unmatched ZIPs (sample): {providers_geo[providers_geo['fips'].isna()]['zip5'].unique()[:10]}")
    print(f"  (These are likely PO Box ZIPs, military APOs, or newer ZIPs not in 2010 Census)")

3. County-Level Network Metrics


Aggregate provider-level network metrics to the county level. For each county we compute:


  • n_obgyn — total OB-GYN providers
  • n_connected — providers with at least one referral connection
  • n_hubs — providers classified as Hub tier
  • mean_degree — average number of referral connections
  • mean_betweenness — average bridge-position score
  • mean_eigenvector — average connection-to-important-providers score
  • pct_isolated — fraction of OB-GYNs with zero connections
In [6]:
# -------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3a. Aggregate Network Metrics by County
# -------------------------------------------------------------------

# Only include providers that matched to a county
geo_valid = providers_geo[providers_geo["fips"].notna()].copy()

county_network = geo_valid.groupby("fips").agg(
    n_obgyn=("npi", "count"),
    n_connected=("is_connected", lambda x: (x == "True").sum() if x.dtype == object else x.sum()),
    n_hubs=("tier", lambda x: (x == "Hub").sum()),
    n_isolated=("tier", lambda x: (x == "Isolated").sum()),
    mean_degree=("total_degree", "mean"),
    median_degree=("total_degree", "median"),
    max_degree=("total_degree", "max"),
    mean_betweenness=("betweenness", "mean"),
    mean_eigenvector=("eigenvector", "mean"),
    mean_weighted_degree=("weighted_degree", "mean"),
    n_subspecialties=("subspecialty", "nunique"),
    dominant_state=("state", lambda x: x.mode().iloc[0] if len(x) > 0 else None)
).reset_index()

county_network["pct_connected"] = (
    county_network["n_connected"] / county_network["n_obgyn"] * 100
).round(1)

county_network["pct_isolated"] = (
    county_network["n_isolated"] / county_network["n_obgyn"] * 100
).round(1)

county_network["pct_hub"] = (
    county_network["n_hubs"] / county_network["n_obgyn"] * 100
).round(1)

print(f"County-level network metrics: {len(county_network):,} counties")
print(f"\nSummary:")
print(county_network[["n_obgyn", "mean_degree", "pct_connected", "pct_isolated"]].describe().round(2).to_string())

4. Join with Morbidity Rates


Merge county network metrics with CDC WONDER morbidity rates on FIPS code. Counties that appear in both datasets are our analysis universe for the geographic overlay.

In [7]:
# -------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4a. Merge Network + Morbidity
# -------------------------------------------------------------------

county_merged = county_network.merge(
    morbidity[["fips", "county_name", "total_births", "morbidity_births", "morbidity_rate", "state"]],
    on="fips",
    how="inner"  # only counties with BOTH network data and morbidity data
)

# Compute provider density per 10K births
county_merged["obgyn_per_10k_births"] = (
    county_merged["n_obgyn"] / county_merged["total_births"] * 10_000
).round(2)

print(f"Counties with both network and morbidity data: {len(county_merged):,}")
print(f"\n  Counties in network only:   {len(county_network) - len(county_merged):,}")
print(f"  Counties in morbidity only: {len(morbidity) - len(county_merged):,}")
print(f"  (Morbidity-only counties may have OB-GYNs with ZIPs that didn't map)")

print(f"\nMerged dataset columns: {list(county_merged.columns)}")
display(county_merged.sort_values("n_obgyn", ascending=False).head(10))

5. Choropleth Maps


Visualize the geographic distribution of provider density, network connectivity, and maternal morbidity. These maps are the visual centerpiece of the blog post.

In [9]:
# -------------------------------------------------------------------
# 5a. Choropleth: Maternal Morbidity Rate by County
# -------------------------------------------------------------------

if HAS_PLOTLY:
    from urllib.request import urlopen
    import json
    
    # Load county GeoJSON for Plotly
    with urlopen('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/plotly/datasets/master/geojson-counties-fips.json') as response:
        counties_geojson = json.load(response)
    
    fig = px.choropleth(
        county_merged,
        geojson=counties_geojson,
        locations="fips",
        color="morbidity_rate",
        color_continuous_scale="YlOrRd",
        scope="usa",
        hover_name="county_name",
        hover_data={
            "morbidity_rate": ":.3f",
            "total_births": ":,.0f",
            "n_obgyn": True,
            "mean_degree": ":.1f",
            "fips": False
        },
        labels={"morbidity_rate": "Morbidity Rate"},
        title="Maternal Morbidity Rate by County (2016)"
    )
    fig.update_layout(margin={"r": 0, "t": 40, "l": 0, "b": 0})
    fig.show()
else:
    # Static fallback: state-level bar chart
    state_morb = county_merged.groupby("state").agg(
        total_births=("total_births", "sum"),
        morbidity_births=("morbidity_births", "sum")
    ).reset_index()
    state_morb["rate"] = state_morb["morbidity_births"] / state_morb["total_births"]
    state_morb = state_morb.sort_values("rate", ascending=True)
    
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 12))
    colors = [PROJECT_COLORS["accent"] if r >= state_morb["rate"].median()
              else PROJECT_COLORS["primary"] for r in state_morb["rate"]]
    ax.barh(state_morb["state"], state_morb["rate"] * 100, color=colors, edgecolor="white")
    ax.set_xlabel("Maternal Morbidity Rate (%)")
    ax.set_title("Maternal Morbidity Rate by State", fontsize=14, fontweight="bold")
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

# -------------------------------------------------------------------
# EXPORT: County-level choropleth data for Tableau (3 maps)
# -------------------------------------------------------------------
# Tableau needs FIPS as a Geographic Role → County for county choropleths.
# One CSV with all fields — use the same data source for all 3 maps,
# just change which field goes on Color.
# -------------------------------------------------------------------

county_map_export = county_merged[[
    "fips", "county_name", "state", "n_obgyn", "n_connected", "n_hubs",
    "n_isolated", "mean_degree", "pct_connected", "pct_isolated", "pct_hub",
    "n_subspecialties", "total_births", "morbidity_births", "morbidity_rate",
    "obgyn_per_10k_births", "mean_betweenness", "mean_weighted_degree"
]].copy()

county_map_export["Morbidity Rate (%)"] = (county_map_export["morbidity_rate"] * 100).round(2)
county_map_export["mean_degree"] = county_map_export["mean_degree"].round(2)
county_map_export["obgyn_per_10k_births"] = county_map_export["obgyn_per_10k_births"].round(1)
county_map_export["pct_connected"] = county_map_export["pct_connected"].round(1)
county_map_export["pct_isolated"] = county_map_export["pct_isolated"].round(1)
county_map_export["mean_betweenness"] = county_map_export["mean_betweenness"].round(6)
county_map_export["mean_weighted_degree"] = county_map_export["mean_weighted_degree"].round(1)

county_map_export = county_map_export.rename(columns={
    "fips": "FIPS",
    "county_name": "County",

# Filter to counties with at least 3 OB-GYNs for more stable metrics
substantial = county_merged[county_merged["n_obgyn"] >= 3].copy()
print(f"Counties with >= 3 OB-GYNs: {len(substantial):,} (of {len(county_merged):,})")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(14, 12))

# (1) Provider density vs morbidity
ax = axes[0, 0]
ax.scatter(substantial["obgyn_per_10k_births"], substantial["morbidity_rate"] * 100,
           s=substantial["total_births"] / 2000, alpha=0.4,
           color=PROJECT_COLORS["primary"], edgecolors="white")
ax.set_xlabel("OB-GYN per 10K Births")
ax.set_ylabel("Morbidity Rate (%)")
ax.set_title("Provider Density vs. Morbidity", fontweight="bold")

# (2) Mean degree vs morbidity
ax = axes[0, 1]
ax.scatter(substantial["mean_degree"], substantial["morbidity_rate"] * 100,
           s=substantial["total_births"] / 2000, alpha=0.4,
           color=PROJECT_COLORS["secondary"], edgecolors="white")
ax.set_xlabel("Mean Network Degree")
ax.set_ylabel("Morbidity Rate (%)")
ax.set_title("Network Connectivity vs. Morbidity", fontweight="bold")

# (3) % Isolated vs morbidity
ax = axes[1, 0]
ax.scatter(substantial["pct_isolated"], substantial["morbidity_rate"] * 100,
           s=substantial["total_births"] / 2000, alpha=0.4,
           color=PROJECT_COLORS["accent"], edgecolors="white")
ax.set_xlabel("% Isolated OB-GYNs")
ax.set_ylabel("Morbidity Rate (%)")
ax.set_title("Provider Isolation vs. Morbidity", fontweight="bold")

# (4) Mean betweenness vs morbidity
ax = axes[1, 1]
ax.scatter(substantial["mean_betweenness"], substantial["morbidity_rate"] * 100,
           s=substantial["total_births"] / 2000, alpha=0.4,
           color=PROJECT_COLORS["highlight"], edgecolors="white")
ax.set_xlabel("Mean Betweenness Centrality")
ax.set_ylabel("Morbidity Rate (%)")
ax.set_title("Bridge Connectivity vs. Morbidity", fontweight="bold")

plt.suptitle("County-Level: Network Metrics vs. Maternal Morbidity Rate",
             fontsize=15, fontweight="bold", y=1.01)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
Counties with >= 3 OB-GYNs: 571 (of 577)

---


6. Regression Analysis — Model Comparison


Can network features predict maternal morbidity? Before answering, we need to:


1. Prepare the data — check distributions, detect outliers, standardize features, test for multicollinearity

2. Fit multiple models — OLS, Weighted Least Squares, Beta Regression, Negative Binomial, GLM Gamma

3. Compare models — using AIC, BIC, R², and diagnostic checks

4. Conclude — which model fits best, and do network variables meaningfully explain morbidity variation?


We use counties with ≥ 3 OB-GYNs (n ≈ 571) for stable county-level metrics.

import statsmodels.api as sm
from statsmodels.stats.outliers_influence import variance_inflation_factor
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

# --- Feature selection ---
feature_vars = [
    "obgyn_per_10k_births", "mean_degree", "pct_isolated",
    "mean_betweenness", "mean_weighted_degree", "n_subspecialties",
    "pct_hub", "n_obgyn"
]

model_data = substantial[["morbidity_rate", "morbidity_births",
                           "total_births"] + feature_vars].dropna().copy()
print(f"Modeling sample: {len(model_data):,} counties\n")

# --- 1. Distribution of dependent variable ---
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(16, 4))

axes[0].hist(model_data["morbidity_rate"], bins=40, color=PROJECT_COLORS["accent"],
             edgecolor="white", alpha=0.8)

axes[0].set_xlabel("Rate")

axes[1].hist(np.log(model_data["morbidity_rate"] + 0.001), bins=40,
             color=PROJECT_COLORS["primary"], edgecolor="white", alpha=0.8)
axes[1].set_title("Log(Morbidity Rate)", fontweight="bold")
axes[1].set_xlabel("Log(Rate)")

axes[2].hist(model_data["morbidity_births"], bins=40,
             color=PROJECT_COLORS["secondary"], edgecolor="white", alpha=0.8)
axes[2].set_title("Morbidity Births (count)", fontweight="bold")
axes[2].set_xlabel("Count")

plt.suptitle("Dependent Variable Distributions", fontsize=14, fontweight="bold")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

skew_raw = model_data["morbidity_rate"].skew()
kurt_raw = model_data["morbidity_rate"].kurtosis()

# -------------------------------------------------------------------
# 6c-3. Standardize Features & Variance Inflation Factor (VIF)
# -------------------------------------------------------------------

# Standardize: mean=0, std=1 for fair coefficient comparison
scaler = StandardScaler()
X_raw = model_data[feature_vars].copy()
X_scaled = pd.DataFrame(
    scaler.fit_transform(X_raw),
    columns=feature_vars,
    index=X_raw.index
)

print("Standardized features (first 5 rows):")
display(X_scaled.head())

# --- VIF: detect multicollinearity ---
# VIF > 5 = moderate concern, VIF > 10 = serious multicollinearity
X_vif = sm.add_constant(X_scaled)
vif_data = pd.DataFrame({
    "Feature": feature_vars,
    "VIF": [variance_inflation_factor(X_vif.values, i+1) for i in range(len(feature_vars))]
}).sort_values("VIF", ascending=False)

vif_data["Flag"] = vif_data["VIF"].apply(
    lambda v: "REMOVE" if v > 10 else ("CAUTION" if v > 5 else "OK"))

print("\nVariance Inflation Factor (VIF) — Multicollinearity Check:")
display(vif_data)

# Drop features with VIF > 10
high_vif = vif_data[vif_data["VIF"] > 10]["Feature"].tolist()
if high_vif:
    print(f"\nDropping high-VIF features: {high_vif}")
    model_features = [f for f in feature_vars if f not in high_vif]
else:
    model_features = feature_vars.copy()

print(f"Final model features ({len(model_features)}): {model_features}")

# Re-standardize with final features
X_final = X_scaled[model_features]
y = model_data["morbidity_rate"]

X_ols = sm.add_constant(X_final)
ols_model = sm.OLS(y, X_ols).fit()

print("MODEL 1: Ordinary Least Squares (Baseline)")

    "Model": "OLS",

    "AIC": round(ols_model.aic, 1),
    "BIC": round(ols_model.bic, 1),
    "F-stat p": f"{ols_model.f_pvalue:.4e}",
    "Sig Features": sum(1 for p in ols_model.pvalues[1:] if p < 0.05),
    "Omnibus p": f"{sm.stats.omni_normtest(ols_model.resid)[1]:.4e}"
})

# 6e. Model 2 — Weighted Least Squares (weighted by birth volume)
# -------------------------------------------------------------------
# Counties with more births give more reliable morbidity estimates.
# Weighting by total_births downweights noisy small-county estimates.
# -------------------------------------------------------------------

X_wls = sm.add_constant(X_final)

# -------------------------------------------------------------------
# 6f. Model 3 — Beta Regression
# -------------------------------------------------------------------
# Morbidity rate is bounded [0, 1] → Beta regression is the natural
# choice for proportional/rate data. It models both the mean and
# precision of the distribution.
#
# Note: Zero-valued rates need a small adjustment since Beta assumes (0,1)
# -------------------------------------------------------------------

from statsmodels.othermod.betareg import BetaModel

# Adjust exact zeros and ones (Beta requires open interval (0,1))
y_beta = model_data["morbidity_rate"].copy()
eps = 1e-6
y_beta = y_beta.clip(lower=eps, upper=1-eps)

X_beta = sm.add_constant(X_final)
beta_model = BetaModel(y_beta, X_beta).fit()

print("MODEL 3: Beta Regression (for proportional data)")
print("=" * 70)
print(beta_model.summary())

# Beta regression uses log-likelihood, AIC, BIC
model_results.append({
    "Model": "Beta Regression",
    "R²": round(beta_model.pseudo_rsquared(), 4) if hasattr(beta_model, 'pseudo_rsquared') else "N/A",
    "Adj R²": "N/A",
    "AIC": round(beta_model.aic, 1),
    "BIC": round(beta_model.bic, 1),
    "F-stat p": "N/A (likelihood)",
    "Sig Features": sum(1 for p in beta_model.pvalues[1:-1] if p < 0.05),
    "Omnibus p": "N/A"
})

print(f"\nBeta regression pseudo-R²: {beta_model.pseudo_rsquared():.4f}" if hasattr(beta_model, 'pseudo_rsquared') else "")

In [22]:
# -------------------------------------------------------------------
# 6g. Model 4 — Negative Binomial (Count Model)
# -------------------------------------------------------------------
# Instead of modeling the rate directly, model morbidity_births as a
# count with log(total_births) as an offset. This respects the count
# nature of the data and handles overdispersion.
# -------------------------------------------------------------------

y_count = model_data["morbidity_births"].astype(int)
offset = np.log(model_data["total_births"])

X_nb = sm.add_constant(X_final)
nb_model = sm.GLM(y_count, X_nb, family=sm.families.NegativeBinomial(alpha=1.0),
                  offset=offset).fit()

print("MODEL 4: Negative Binomial (count model with birth offset)")
print("=" * 70)
print(nb_model.summary())

# Compute pseudo R-squared (McFadden)
null_model = sm.GLM(y_count, np.ones(len(y_count)),
                    family=sm.families.NegativeBinomial(alpha=1.0),
                    offset=offset).fit()
pseudo_r2_nb = 1 - (nb_model.llf / null_model.llf)

model_results.append({
    "Model": "Negative Binomial",
    "R²": round(pseudo_r2_nb, 4),

In [23]:
# -------------------------------------------------------------------
# 6h. Model 5 — GLM with Gamma Family (log link)
# -------------------------------------------------------------------
# For strictly positive, right-skewed continuous data.
# Gamma GLM with log link is a common choice for rate/cost data.
# Requires y > 0, so we filter out zero-morbidity counties.
# -------------------------------------------------------------------

positive_mask = model_data["morbidity_rate"] > 0
model_data_pos = model_data[positive_mask]
y_gamma = model_data_pos["morbidity_rate"]
X_gamma = sm.add_constant(X_final.loc[positive_mask])

gamma_model = sm.GLM(y_gamma, X_gamma,
                     family=sm.families.Gamma(link=sm.families.links.Log())).fit()

print(f"MODEL 5: GLM Gamma (log link) — {len(model_data_pos)} counties with morbidity > 0")
print("=" * 70)
print(gamma_model.summary())

# Pseudo R-squared (deviance-based)
null_gamma = sm.GLM(y_gamma, np.ones(len(y_gamma)),
                    family=sm.families.Gamma(link=sm.families.links.Log())).fit()
pseudo_r2_gamma = 1 - (gamma_model.deviance / null_gamma.deviance)

model_results.append({
    "Model": "GLM Gamma (log link)",
    "R²": round(pseudo_r2_gamma, 4),
    "Adj R²": "N/A",
    "AIC": round(gamma_model.aic, 1),
    "BIC": round(gamma_model.bic, 1),
    "F-stat p": "N/A (likelihood)",
    "Sig Features": sum(1 for p in gamma_model.pvalues[1:] if p < 0.05),
    "Omnibus p": "N/A"
})

print(f"\nPseudo R² (deviance): {pseudo_r2_gamma:.4f}")

# -------------------------------------------------------------------
# 6j. Diagnostic Plots — OLS Baseline
# -------------------------------------------------------------------
# Even though OLS may not be the best model, diagnostics on the OLS
# residuals illustrate WHY alternative models are needed.
# -------------------------------------------------------------------

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(14, 10))

# 1. Residuals vs Fitted
fitted = ols_model.fittedvalues
resid = ols_model.resid
axes[0, 0].scatter(fitted, resid, alpha=0.4, s=15, color=PROJECT_COLORS["primary"])
axes[0, 0].axhline(y=0, color="red", linestyle="--")
axes[0, 0].set_xlabel("Fitted Values")
axes[0, 0].set_ylabel("Residuals")
axes[0, 0].set_title("Residuals vs Fitted", fontweight="bold")

# 2. Q-Q Plot
from scipy.stats import probplot
probplot(resid, dist="norm", plot=axes[0, 1])
axes[0, 1].set_title("Q-Q Plot (Normality Check)", fontweight="bold")
axes[0, 1].get_lines()[0].set_color(PROJECT_COLORS["primary"])
axes[0, 1].get_lines()[1].set_color("red")

# 3. Scale-Location (sqrt of standardized residuals)
std_resid = ols_model.get_influence().resid_studentized_internal
axes[1, 0].scatter(fitted, np.sqrt(np.abs(std_resid)), alpha=0.4, s=15,
                   color=PROJECT_COLORS["accent"])
axes[1, 0].set_xlabel("Fitted Values")
axes[1, 0].set_ylabel("√|Standardized Residuals|")
axes[1, 0].set_title("Scale-Location (Homoscedasticity)", fontweight="bold")

# 4. Residuals histogram
axes[1, 1].hist(resid, bins=50, color=PROJECT_COLORS["primary"],
                edgecolor="white", alpha=0.8)
axes[1, 1].set_xlabel("Residuals")
axes[1, 1].set_ylabel("Frequency")
axes[1, 1].set_title("Residual Distribution", fontweight="bold")
axes[1, 1].axvline(0, color="red", linestyle="--")

plt.suptitle("OLS Diagnostic Plots — Why Alternative Models Are Needed",
             fontsize=14, fontweight="bold")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# Formal tests
from statsmodels.stats.diagnostic import het_breuschpagan, acorr_ljungbox
from scipy.stats import shapiro

bp_stat, bp_p, _, _ = het_breuschpagan(resid, X_ols)
# Shapiro-Wilk on a subsample (max 5000)
sw_stat, sw_p = shapiro(resid[:5000]) if len(resid) > 5000 else shapiro(resid)

print("OLS Diagnostic Tests:")
print(f"  Breusch-Pagan (heteroscedasticity): stat={bp_stat:.3f}, p={bp_p:.4e}")
print(f"    {'FAIL — residuals have non-constant variance' if bp_p < 0.05 else 'PASS — homoscedasticity OK'}")
print(f"  Shapiro-Wilk (normality):           stat={sw_stat:.3f}, p={sw_p:.4e}")
print(f"    {'FAIL — residuals are not normally distributed' if sw_p < 0.05 else 'PASS — normality OK'}")
print(f"  Durbin-Watson (autocorrelation):    {sm.stats.durbin_watson(resid):.3f}")
print(f"    (Near 2.0 = no autocorrelation)")

# -------------------------------------------------------------------
# 6k. Conclusion: Do Network Variables Explain Morbidity?
# -------------------------------------------------------------------

print("=" * 75)
print("REGRESSION ANALYSIS — CONCLUSIONS")
print("=" * 75)

print(f"""
1. DATA PREPARATION
   - Sample: {len(model_data):,} counties with ≥ 3 OB-GYNs
   - Features standardized (mean=0, std=1) for fair comparison
   - VIF check: {len(high_vif)} features dropped for multicollinearity
   - Final features: {len(model_features)}

2. KEY FINDING: Network variables do NOT meaningfully predict
   county-level maternal morbidity rates.
   
   - Across ALL 5 models, R² / pseudo-R² remains below 0.03
   - No network variable consistently achieves p < 0.05
   - The best-fitting model ({best_model}) still explains
     very little variance in morbidity

3. WHY THIS MATTERS (for your interview):
   
   a) This is a VALID and IMPORTANT finding — null results are real results
   b) Possible explanations:
      - Morbidity is driven by socioeconomic factors (poverty, insurance,
        race) that our network data doesn't capture
      - The Medicare-based network is a proxy for OB-GYN infrastructure,
        not direct obstetric patient flow
      - County-level aggregation may mask provider-level effects
      - The CDC WONDER data only covers large counties (100K+ pop),
        excluding the most rural/underserved areas
   
   c) What the network analysis DOES show:
      - 80% of OB-GYNs are isolated (no shared patient connections)
      - Care coordination is concentrated in a small number of hubs
      - Geographic variation in network structure is real and measurable
      - Target counties combine high morbidity WITH weak networks,
        even if the causal link isn't proven by regression

4. MODEL SELECTION RATIONALE:
   - OLS: baseline, but residuals violate normality & homoscedasticity
   - WLS: accounts for county size, slight improvement
   - Beta regression: theoretically correct for proportional data
   - Negative Binomial: respects count nature, handles overdispersion
   - GLM Gamma: handles right-skewed positive continuous outcomes

5. RECOMMENDED NEXT STEPS (if this were a production analysis):
   - Add socioeconomic controls (Census ACS poverty, insurance, race data)
   - Use spatial regression to account for geographic clustering
   - Analyze at the provider level rather than county aggregation
   - Incorporate Medicaid claims data for actual obstetric patient flow
""")

# Export conclusion summary for Tableau
conclusion_rows = [
    {"Finding": "Network variables predict morbidity", "Result": "No",
     "Detail": f"R² < 0.03 across all {len(model_results)} models"},
    {"Finding": "Best model", "Result": best_model,
     "Detail": "Lowest AIC among fitted models"},
    {"Finding": "OB-GYNs isolated", "Result": "80%",
     "Detail": "No shared patient connections in CMS data"},
    {"Finding": "Target counties identified", "Result": "See Section 7",
     "Detail": "High morbidity + weak network overlap"},
    {"Finding": "Key limitation", "Result": "Missing confounders",
     "Detail": "Poverty, insurance, race not in model"},
]
conclusion_df = pd.DataFrame(conclusion_rows)
conclusion_df.to_csv(OUTPUT_DIR / "tableau_regression_conclusions.csv", index=False)
print(f"\nSaved: {OUTPUT_DIR / 'tableau_regression_conclusions.csv'}")
display(conclusion_df)

7. Target County Identification


Identify counties that combine high maternal morbidity with weak referral networks — these represent the highest-opportunity areas for virtual care interventions like Pomelo Care's model.


Criteria:

  • Morbidity rate in the top quartile (above 75th percentile)
  • At least one of: mean degree in bottom quartile, or % isolated in top quartile, or fewer than 5 OB-GYNs

isolated_q75 = county_merged["pct_isolated"].quantile(0.75)

print(f"  Mean degree <= {degree_q25:.1f} — bottom quartile")
print(f"  % Isolated >= {isolated_q75:.1f}% — top quartile")

# -------------------------------------------------------------------
# 7b. Identify Target Counties
# -------------------------------------------------------------------

high_morb = county_merged["morbidity_rate"] >= morb_q75

weak_network = (
    (county_merged["mean_degree"] <= degree_q25) |
    (county_merged["pct_isolated"] >= isolated_q75) |
    (county_merged["n_obgyn"] < 5)
)

target_counties = county_merged[high_morb & weak_network].copy()
target_counties = target_counties.sort_values("morbidity_rate", ascending=False)

print(f"Target counties (high morbidity + weak network): {len(target_counties):,}")
print(f"  Total births in target counties: {target_counties['total_births'].sum():,.0f}")

# -------------------------------------------------------------------
# EXPORT: Target vs Non-Target comparison for Tableau table
# -------------------------------------------------------------------

comparison_metrics = [
    ("Morbidity Rate (%)", "morbidity_rate", 100),
    ("OB-GYN per 10K Births", "obgyn_per_10k_births", 1),
    ("Mean Degree", "mean_degree", 1),
    ("Pct Isolated (%)", "pct_isolated", 1),
    ("Pct Hub (%)", "pct_hub", 1),
    ("Total OB-GYNs", "n_obgyn", 1),
    ("Total Births", "total_births", 1),
    ("Mean Betweenness", "mean_betweenness", 1),
]

comp_rows = []
for label, var, multiplier in comparison_metrics:
    t_val = target_counties[var].mean() * multiplier
    nt_val = non_target[var].mean() * multiplier
    if nt_val != 0:
        diff_pct = ((t_val - nt_val) / nt_val * 100)
    else:
        diff_pct = 0
    comp_rows.append({
        "Metric": label,
        "Target Counties": round(t_val, 2),
        "Non-Target Counties": round(nt_val, 2),
        "Difference (%)": f"{diff_pct:+.1f}%"
    })

comp_export = pd.DataFrame(comp_rows)
comp_export.to_csv(OUTPUT_DIR / "tableau_target_vs_nontarget.csv", index=False)
print(f"Saved: {OUTPUT_DIR / 'tableau_target_vs_nontarget.csv'}")
display(comp_export)

Interpretation Notes for Blog Post


What the data can support

  • Geographic variation in OB-GYN network connectivity is real and measurable
  • Some counties have dense, well-connected referral networks; others have isolated or sparse provider coverage
  • Maternal morbidity rates vary substantially by county
  • The association between network features and morbidity provides directional signals worth exploring

What to be careful about

  • Correlation ≠ causation — weak networks don't necessarily cause worse outcomes; both may be driven by shared upstream factors (rural poverty, hospital closures, insurance coverage gaps)
  • Medicare-driven network — the referral patterns reflect Medicare (primarily elderly gynecology) patient sharing, not obstetric patient flow directly. Evidence suggests >80% of OB-GYNs see both Medicare and Medicaid patients, so the network infrastructure is likely shared
  • County matching limitations — ZIP-to-county mapping is approximate; some providers practice near county borders
  • CDC WONDER population threshold — only counties with 100K+ population have individual morbidity data; smaller rural counties (potentially the most underserved) are grouped into "Unidentified"

Pomelo Care framing

  • Target counties represent areas where virtual care could fill coordination gaps
  • The network topology reveals where care coordination infrastructure is weakest, even if the patient population driving the edges skews older
  • Providers in isolated or low-degree positions could benefit most from virtual specialist access
